title: Losing Money on Purpose
intro: You asked the board a good question two meetings ago. Today you answer it yourself.

blocks.html:
Here was your question.

Amazon lost money for years.

It grew into one of the biggest companies on earth.

How can losing money be a plan?

Today you settle it — using a company small enough to fit on one page.

Riverbend Books. An online bookshop. Three years of accounts.

blocks.hint: Money in minus money out. Money out is bigger here, so the answer drops below zero.

parts.label: Profit (£, use a minus sign)
parts._working: 100 − 120 = −20. A loss of £20. (Unit 1's negatives, still earning their keep.)

blocks.prompt:
Forget the losses for a moment. Look only at the revenue — the money coming in.

The shop made £100 in its first year, £200 in its second year, and £400 in its third year.
 Year 1Year 2Year 3
Revenue£100£200£400
blocks.hint: What is happening to the number each year? Then do that once more.

parts.label: Year 4 revenue, if it carries on (£)
parts._working: Each year is twice the year before: 100 → 200 → 400 → 800.

parts.label: What is the revenue doing each year? (one word)
parts._working: Doubling. Accept list is deliberately wide: "growing" and "going up" are true and a child who writes them has understood the point, so they must not be marked wrong. The precise word wanted is doubling.

blocks.button: Why a loss can be a plan ✨
blocks.html:
Riverbend is losing money.

Riverbend is also doubling.

Every £1 of that loss went on something: a warehouse, a delivery van, a cheaper price to win a customer off a rival.

The loss is not a wound.

It is a purchase.

So an analyst asks two questions about a loss-making company, and only two:

1. Is it getting bigger, fast?

2. Could it stop spending and make a profit whenever it wanted to?

blocks.prompt:
Here are the full accounts. Your job is the profit line.

In year 1 the shop made £100 and spent £120. In year 2 it made £200 and spent £210. In year 3 it made £400 and spent £320.
 Year 1Year 2Year 3
Revenue (money in)£100£200£400
Costs (money out)£120£210£320
blocks.hint: One year at a time. Year 2 is still a loss — but look at its size next to Year 1's.

parts.label: Year 2 profit (£)
parts._working: 200 − 210 = −10. Still a loss, but half the size of Year 1's £20 loss.

parts.label: Year 3 profit (£)
parts._working: 400 − 320 = +80. The loss shrank, then flipped into a real profit. That shape — shrinking loss, growing revenue — is the whole story of the session.

blocks.prompt: Two analyst's numbers on that third year.
blocks.hint: Margin: compare the £80 profit to the £320 it cost. Then add all three years together — minus signs and all.

parts.label: Year 3 margin (%)
parts._working: 80/320 = 8/32 = 1/4 = 25%. Gear check: a quarter of 320 is 80 ✓. Decimal twin 0.25 is included because the engine reads a typed "25%" as 0.25.

parts.label: All three years added up (£)
parts._working: (−20) + (−10) + 80 = −30 + 80 = +50. Three years of accounts, £50 to show for it — and a business four times bigger than it started.

blocks.prompt:
Boss question. Two companies land on your desk. Both of them are losing money.

In year 1, Company A makes £50 of revenue and loses £10. In year 2 it makes £100 and loses only £5.

Company B makes £50 of revenue in year 1 and loses £10. In year 2 it makes £50 again, and loses £20.
 Year 1Year 2
Company A revenue£50£100
Company A loss£10£5
Company B revenue£50£50
Company B loss£10£20
blocks.hint: Ask your two questions about each one: is it growing, and is the loss getting smaller? Then push B's loss on one more year the way it's going.

parts.label: B's loss next year, if it carries on (£)
parts._working: B's loss is doubling: 10 → 20 → 40. Accept both 40 and −40 — the label says "loss", so a child who writes the size (40) and one who writes it as a negative profit (−40) are both right.

parts.label: Which one is losing money on purpose? (A or B)
parts._working: A. Its revenue doubled while its loss halved — it is buying growth and could clearly stop. B's revenue stood still while its loss doubled — that is not a plan, that is just losing money.

blocks.prompt:
★ A rival shop copies the plan. But its losses never get any smaller.

In year 1 it loses £20. In year 2 it loses £30. In year 3 it loses £40.
 Year 1Year 2Year 3
Loss that year£20£30£40
It borrows money to cover every loss. Its lender will only keep waiting until the borrowing adds up to £100.
blocks.hint: Add the losses up as you go: after Year 1, then after Year 2, then after Year 3. Year 4's loss carries the pattern on — the losses grow by £10 each year.

parts.label: Add up the losses from years 1, 2 and 3. How much has it borrowed in total? (£)
parts._working: 20 + 30 = 50 after Year 2; 50 + 40 = 90 after Year 3. Still under the £100 limit — but only just.

parts.label: In which year does the borrowing go past £100? (just the year number)
parts._working: Year 4's loss continues the pattern: £50. Borrowing goes 90 + 50 = £140, well past the lender's £100 limit. So it runs out in Year 4. Label says "just the number" because the engine cannot read "year 4" as a number.

blocks.html:
📈 The analyst's verdict — for the dinner table:

Amazon lost money for years and became one of the biggest companies on earth.

Hundreds of other companies lost money for years and vanished.

Same strategy. Opposite endings.

Here is your job tonight. You may ask a loss-making company one question only before deciding. What is it?

Then put this to Dad: in 1997 Amazon was a small website that sold books and lost money. Would he have put £100 into it?

And the harder half — would he still have had it there ten years later?

(Most people say yes to the first and no to the second. That second one is the difficult part of investing, and almost nobody talks about it.)

done.title: UNIT 2 COMPLETE 🍋✓
done.html:
Sales & Margins is closed. Revenue, costs, profit and loss. The margin that judges a profit, and the trap inside it. And now the hardest call of the lot — telling a company that is losing money on purpose from a company that is simply losing money.

Most adults cannot do that. You just did it with three years of accounts and two questions.
